claim: In the Drosophila circadian clock, Period (PER) and Timeless (TIM) proteins inhibit Clock-mediated transcription of per and tim genes until PER is degraded by Doubletime/CK1 (DBT)-mediated phosphorylation, establishing a negative feedback loop.
source: In the Drosophila circadian clock, Period (PER) and Timeless (TIM) proteins inhibit Clock-mediated transcription of per and tim genes until PER is degraded by Doubletime/CK1 (DBT)-mediated phosphorylation, establishing a negative feedback loop.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the basic mechanism of the Drosophila circadian clock, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Multiple regulatory delays within the circadian feedback loop ensure ~24 hr periodicity.
source: Multiple regulatory delays within this feedback loop ensure ~24 hr periodicity.
evidence: This is a general statement about circadian clock mechanisms, representing established knowledge.

claim: Phosphorylation of PER residue S589 stabilizes and activates PER inhibitory function in the presence of TIM.
source: Our results indicate that phosphorylation of PER residue S589 stabilizes and activates PER inhibitory function in the presence of TIM, but promotes PER degradation in its absence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including pulse-chase assays (Figure 3) and transcription assays (Figure 5).

claim: Phosphorylation of PER residue S589 promotes PER degradation in the absence of TIM.
source: Our results indicate that phosphorylation of PER residue S589 stabilizes and activates PER inhibitory function in the presence of TIM, but promotes PER degradation in its absence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of S589 phosphorylation depending on TIM presence (Figures 2, 3).

claim: The role of DBT in regulating PER activity, stabilization and degradation ensures that these events are chronologically and biochemically linked.
source: The role of DBT in regulating PER activity, stabilization and degradation ensures that these events are chronologically and biochemically linked, and contributes to the timing of an essential delay that influences the period of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The activator complex in Drosophila circadian clock consists of dClock/Cycle (dCLK/CYC), which initiates transcription of period (per) and timeless (tim).
source: In Drosophila, the activator complex consists of dClock/Cycle (dCLK/CYC), which initiates transcription of period (per) and timeless (tim).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila circadian clock mechanism.

claim: PER and TIM proteins assemble to form an inhibitory complex in the cytoplasm that, after a delay, enters the nucleus to inhibit dCLK/CYC activity.
source: PER and TIM proteins assemble to form an inhibitory complex in the cytoplasm that, after a delay, enters the nucleus to inhibit dCLK/CYC activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila circadian clock mechanism.

claim: After a delay, the PER/TIM inhibitory complex is degraded, freeing the activator complex to reinitiate transcription, closing the feedback loop.
source: After a second delay, the inhibitory complex is degraded, freeing the activator complex to reinitiate transcription, closing the feedback loop.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila circadian clock mechanism.

claim: The delay in transcriptional activation is critical for maintaining ~24 hr rhythmicity.
source: Although the delay in transcriptional activation is critical for maintaining ~24 hr rhythmicity, its regulatory mechanisms are not well understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the circadian clock field.

claim: A Casein Kinase I/Doubletime (DBT) phosphorylation cascade on PER regulates PER protein stability.
source: A Casein Kinase I/Doubletime (DBT) phosphorylation cascade on PER regulates PER protein stability.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Each DBT phosphorylation event gates later phosphorylation events on PER, thus delaying protein degradation and transcriptional activation.
source: Current models of this phosphorylation cascade infer that each DBT phosphorylation event gates later phosphorylation events on PER, thus delaying protein degradation and transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is a description of current models in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: The phosphorylation cascade begins with the PER Short Downstream region (PER-SD, amino acids 604–629), which promotes S47 phosphorylation.
source: The cascade begins with the PER Short Downstream region (PER-SD, amino acids 604–629), which promotes S47 phosphorylation (Garbe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of S47 is a necessary modification to trigger ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of PER by the E3-ligase SLIMB.
source: Phosphorylation of S47, is a necessary modification to trigger ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of PER by the E3-ligase SLIMB (Chiu et al., 2008; Garbe et al., 2013; Kivimäe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PER-SD blocks NEMO kinase from phosphorylating S596.
source: PER-SD also blocks NEMO kinase from phosphorylating S596.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: NEMO phosphorylation of S596 promotes S589 phosphorylation by DBT, which blocks S47 phosphorylation.
source: By phosphorylating S596, NEMO promotes S589 phosphorylation by DBT, which blocks S47 phosphorylation (Chiu et al., 2011; Garbe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PER-SD phosphorylation removes the S589-mediated negative regulation of S47 phosphorylation while independently promoting S47 phosphorylation.
source: In other words, PER-SD phosphorylation removes the S589-mediated negative regulation of S47 phosphorylation while independently promoting S47 phosphorylation (Garbe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mutation of the S589 site in flies leads to a short behavioral period.
source: Mutation of the S589 site in flies leads to a short behavioral period (Baylies et al., 1992; Konopka and Benzer, 1971; Rutila et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S589 is a DBT phosphorylation site.
source: Given that S589 is a DBT phosphorylation site (Chiu et al., 2008; Kivimäe et al., 2008), it is surprising that mutations that both block (Gly) and substitute for phosphorylation (Asp) lead to a short behavioral rhythm (Rutila et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations that both block (Gly) and substitute for phosphorylation (Asp) at S589 lead to a short behavioral rhythm.
source: Given that S589 is a DBT phosphorylation site (Chiu et al., 2008; Kivimäe et al., 2008), it is surprising that mutations that both block (Gly) and substitute for phosphorylation (Asp) lead to a short behavioral rhythm (Rutila et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The behavioral period of the S589D phosphomimetic is longer than a mutant that prevents phosphorylation (Gly).
source: Although this may suggest that the aspartate residue substitution does not serve as an effective phosphomimetic, the fact that the behavioral period of the mimetic is longer than a mutant that prevents phosphorylation (Gly) suggests a more complex regulatory mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous observations cited in the text.

claim: TIM binding to PER protects PER from hyperphosphorylation and degradation.
source: TIM binding to PER adds another layer of complexity to the model by protecting PER from hyperphosphorylation and degradation (Kloss et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The DBT phosphorylation cascade on PER is influenced by TIM.
source: This suggests that the DBT phosphorylation cascade on PER is influenced by TIM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TIM protects PER from hyperphosphorylation.

claim: PER phosphorylation, PER degradation and PER inhibitory activity coincide closely in time and space.
source: PER phosphorylation, PER degradation and PER inhibitory activity coincide closely in time and space (Abruzzi et al., 2011; Edery et al., 1994), which has led to a model in which PER stability and inhibitory activity are regulated by the same regulatory mechanism (Kivimäe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A phosphonull alanine substitution at S589 (S589A) caused an advance in evening anticipation but not morning anticipation relative to controls in a 12:12 light/dark (LD) light regiment.
source: As previously reported (Baylies et al., 1992; Rutila et al., 1992), a phosphonull alanine substitution (S589A) caused an advance in evening anticipation but not morning anticipation relative to controls in a 12:12 light/dark (LD) light regiment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and confirmed by previous studies.

claim: S589A mutants exhibited a ~ 6 hr shorter period in activity rhythm relative to controls in constant darkness.
source: In constant darkness (DD), S589A mutants exhibited a ~ 6 hr shorter period in activity rhythm relative to controls (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1; ~19.5 hr S589A vs ~25.5 hr wild type).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Phosphomimetic S589D mutants exhibit a modest advance in evening anticipation and no change in morning anticipation relative to controls.
source: Similar to phosphonull S589A mutants, we found that phosphomimetic S589D mutants exhibit a modest advance in evening anticipation and no change in morning anticipation relative to controls (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The activity period of S589D in constant darkness was shortened, leading to a ~ 2 hr shorter subjective day.
source: Consistent with this result, the activity period of S589D in DD was also shortened, leading to a ~ 2 hr shorter subjective day (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1; 23.5 h S589D vs ~25.5 hr wild type).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Both S589 mutations blocked the effect of DBT overexpression on period length.
source: We found that both S589 mutations blocked this effect of DBT overexpression on period length (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DBT overexpression in transgenic flies expressing wild type PER caused a modest increase in period length of ~1 hr.
source: DBT overexpression in transgenic flies expressing wild type PER caused a modest increase in period length of ~1 hr, as expected (Muskus et al., 2007; Venkatesan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and confirmed by previous studies.

claim: The ability of S589 to block the effect of DBT overexpression on behavior suggests that its modification occurs before other functions of DBT that regulate behavior.
source: The ability of S589 to block the effect of DBT overexpression on behavior suggests that its modification occurs before other functions of DBT that regulate behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: The ability of S589 to curb the effect of DBT overexpression provides evidence that S589 and DBT genetically interact.
source: The ability of S589 to curb the effect of DBT overexpression also provides evidence that S589 and DBT genetically interact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: OGT overexpression in wild type flies lengthened rhythmic behavior of wild type flies.
source: We found that OGT overexpression in wild type flies lengthened rhythmic behavior of wild type flies, as expected (Kaasik et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and confirmed by previous studies.

claim: OGT overexpression in the S589A and S589D mutant backgrounds similarly lengthened rhythmic behavior of the mutant flies.
source: The same experiment conducted in the S589A and S589D mutant backgrounds similarly lengthened rhythmic behavior of the mutant flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: S589 does not genetically interact with OGT.
source: We therefore conclude that S589 does not genetically interact with OGT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing OGT overexpression affects all genotypes similarly.

claim: Mutant forms of dbt that reduce DBT kinase activity produce long (dbtL) and short (dbtS) behavioral rhythms.
source: Mutant forms of dbt that reduce DBT kinase activity produce long (dbtL) and short (dbtS) behavioral rhythms (Kivimäe et al., 2008; Preuss et al., 2004; Price et al., 1998), suggesting that DBT may play two roles in regulating PER.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In cultured cells dbtL is defective in regulating PER stability, whereas dbtS is not associated with regulating PER stability.
source: Indeed, in cultured cells dbtL is defective in regulating PER stability, whereas dbtS is not associated with regulating PER stability (Syed et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of either phosphonull (S589A) or phosphomimetic (S589D) per variants in a dbtL genetic background leads to longer behavioral rhythms.
source: We found that expression of either phosphonull (S589A) or phosphomimetic (S589D) per variants in a dbtL genetic background leads to longer behavioral rhythms (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of wild type per in a dbtS genetic background leads to a shorter behavioral rhythm of wt flies, but not of the S589 mutants.
source: In contrast, expression of wild type per in a dbtS genetic background leads to a shorter behavioral rhythm of wt flies, but not of the S589 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mutations of S589 block the period changes caused by dbtS but not dbtL.
source: Thus, mutations of S589 block the period changes caused by dbtS but not dbtL, suggesting that the S589 mutations and dbtS lie within the same regulatory pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: dbtS, which has reduced kinase activity, delays PER nuclear accumulation in vivo.
source: dbtS, which has reduced kinase activity, delays PER nuclear accumulation in vivo (Bao et al., 2001; Kivimäe et al., 2008; Rothenfluh et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The original PERS mutant protein (S589N) exhibits kinetics of nuclear entry similar to wild type.
source: Although the original PERS mutant protein (S589N) exhibits kinetics of nuclear entry similar to wild type (Curtin et al., 1995), because S589 phosphomutants and dbtS genetically interact, we first tested whether S589 phosphomutations alter the kinetics of PER/TIM nuclear accumulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: S589 mutants did not alter the kinetics of nuclear accumulation of PER or TIM in the small LNvs relative to controls.
source: Similar to the original PERS mutant, we found that S589 mutants did not alter the kinetics of nuclear accumulation of PER or TIM in the small LNvs (Figure 2B) or the large LNvs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) relative to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Residue substitutions of S589 do not shorten period length by changing the rate of nuclear accumulation of the PER/TIM inhibitory complex.
source: Thus, residue substitutions of S589 do not shorten period length by changing the rate of nuclear accumulation of the PER/TIM inhibitory complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the nuclear accumulation data.

claim: S589 phosphorylation regulates PER function after nuclear entry.
source: This result further suggests that S589 phosphorylation regulates PER function after nuclear entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that S589 mutations do not affect nuclear accumulation.

claim: The phosphonull S589A substitution does not affect PER stability between ZT20 and CT02, but destabilizes PER after CT02.
source: The phosphonull S589A substitution does not affect PER stability between ZT20 and CT02, but destabilizes PER after CT02, leading to a gradual loss of PER protein relative to controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TIM is destabilized in the S589A genetic background compared to wild type.
source: TIM is similarly destabilized in the S589A genetic background compared to wild type (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The phosphomimetic S589D mutant behaves like wild-type PER until TIM is degraded at CT06, at which time the PER S589D protein is rapidly degraded compared to wild type.
source: In contrast, the phosphomimetic S589D mutant behaves like wild-type PER until TIM is degraded at CT06, at which time the PER S589D protein is rapidly degraded compared to wild type (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The changes in the stability of the PER variants correlate well with the differences in rhythmic behavior exhibited by the relevant fly mutants.
source: The changes in the stability of the PER variants correlate well with the differences in rhythmic behavior exhibited by the relevant fly mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the stability data (Figure 2) with behavioral data (Figure 1B).

claim: S589 phosphorylation is required to stabilize the PER/TIM inhibitory complex after CT02 in the small LNvs.
source: These data suggest that S589 phosphorylation is required to stabilize the PER/TIM inhibitory complex after CT02 in the small LNvs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stability data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Upon TIM degradation, phosphorylation at S589 promotes PER degradation, ending the transcriptional inhibitory phase of the circadian clock.
source: However, upon TIM degradation, the behavior of S589D indicates that phosphorylation at S589 now promotes PER degradation, ending the transcriptional inhibitory phase of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that S589D is rapidly degraded after TIM degradation.

claim: Phosphorylation at S589 both stabilizes and destabilizes PER at different points in the circadian cycle, depending on the presence or absence of TIM protein.
source: That is, phosphorylation at S589 both stabilizes and destabilizes PER at different points in the circadian cycle, depending on the presence or absence of TIM protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of S589 phosphorylation in the presence and absence of TIM.

claim: S589 phosphorylation has a stabilizing effect when TIM is present.
source: Thus, S589 phosphorylation has a stabilizing effect when TIM is present.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stability data in the presence of TIM.

claim: Analysis of the S589N variant of PER (PERS) in a study that included TIM (but not DBT) in cultured cells suggests that it is equivalent in stability to wild type PER.
source: Analysis of the S589N variant of PER (PERS) in a similar study that included TIM (but not DBT) in cultured cells suggests that it is equivalent in stability to wild type PER (Li and Rosbash, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The phosphonull S589A mutation destabilizes PER relative to wild-type PER in the presence of DBT.
source: Using this assay, we found that the phosphonull S589A mutation destabilizes PER relative to wild-type PER in the presence of DBT (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phosphorylation of S589 on PER normally protects PER from DBT-mediated degradation in a complex with TIM.
source: This result suggests that phosphorylation of S589 on PER normally protects PER from DBT-mediated degradation in a complex with TIM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pulse-chase assay data.

claim: S589 phosphorylation is not required to complete the PER phosphorylation cascade to promote PER degradation.
source: This result also suggests that S589 phosphorylation is not required to complete the PER phosphorylation cascade to promote PER degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that S589A mutant PER is destabilized.

claim: PER protein containing the phosphomimetic S589D mutation exhibits stability similar to wild type in the presence of DBT activity.
source: Consistent with this finding, PER protein containing the phosphomimetic S589D mutation exhibits stability similar to wild type in the presence of DBT activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DBT activity inhibits PER degradation at the stage when PER is in complex with TIM.
source: The S589D result also suggests that DBT activity inhibits PER degradation at this stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that S589D (phosphomimetic) is stable in the presence of DBT.

claim: TIM stability follows the same pattern as the PER variants; destabilized by the PER phosphonull variant (S589A) but not the PER phosphomimetic (S589D), compared to controls.
source: TIM stability in this assay follows the same pattern as the PER variants; destabilized by the PER phosphonull variant (S589A) but not the PER phosphomimetic (S589D), compared to controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the absence of TIM, PER exhibits rapid degradation that is not quantifiable over time.
source: This assay repeated in the absence of TIM reveals rapid PER degradation that is not quantifiable over time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: S589 phosphorylation stabilizes PER in the presence of TIM from DBT-mediated degradation, either by blocking phosphorylation of other PER destabilizing sites, or in spite of phosphorylation of these other sites.
source: These data therefore suggest that S589 phosphorylation stabilizes PER in the presence of TIM from DBT-mediated degradation, either by blocking phosphorylation of other PER destabilizing sites, or in spite of phosphorylation of these other sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pulse-chase assay data.

claim: Blocking S589 phosphorylation redirects DBT to promote the degradation of the PER/TIM complex, likely by phosphorylating other PER sites.
source: In contrast, blocking S589 phosphorylation redirects DBT to promote the degradation of the PER/TIM complex, likely by phosphorylating other PER sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that S589A is destabilized.

claim: S589 acts to direct DBT to degrade PER or to stabilize PER within the PER/TIM complex.
source: Therefore S589 acts to direct DBT to degrade PER or to stabilize PER within the PER/TIM complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of S589 phosphorylation state.

claim: DBT-mediated degradation of PER occurs in both the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: DBT-mediated degradation of PER occurs in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (Price et al., 1998; Venkatesan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When PER and TIM are restricted to the cytoplasm, wild type PER and PER S589A are similar in their stability.
source: When PER and TIM are restricted to the cytoplasm, wild type PER and PER S589A are similar in their stability (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Lack of phosphorylation at S589 destabilizes PER specifically in the nucleus.
source: Thus, lack of phosphorylation at S589 destabilizes PER specifically in the nucleus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing nuclear and cytoplasmic stability data.

claim: S589D is more stable than wild type PER in the cytoplasm.
source: As a side note, S589D is more stable than wild type PER in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Phosphorylation of S589 is required for stabilization of PER in the presence of TIM.
source: Our data further suggest that phosphorylation of S589 is required for stabilization of PER in the presence of TIM.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stability data in the presence of TIM.

claim: Both S589A and S589D mutants have shorter total periods than control flies expressing the wild type per transgene.
source: Both S589A and S589D mutants have shorter total periods than control flies expressing the wild type per transgene.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The period of bioluminescence oscillation correlates well with behavioral period.
source: Thus, the period of bioluminescence oscillation correlates well with behavioral period (Figures 4B and 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing bioluminescence data (Figure 4B) with behavioral data (Figure 1C).

claim: The dCLK active phase of S589A mutants is shorter than both wild type and S589D, which are equivalent.
source: This analysis revealed that the dCLK active phase of S589A mutants is shorter than both wild type and S589D, which are equivalent (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The dCLK inactive phase of S589A and S589D mutants are equivalent to each other and shorter than wild type.
source: On the other hand, the dCLK inactive phase of S589A and S589D mutants are equivalent to each other and shorter than wild type (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The dCLK inactive phase is shortened in both S589A and S589D mutants, consistent with the role of this residue in regulating PER stability.
source: These data suggest that the dCLK inactive phase is shortened in both S589A and S589D mutants, consistent with the role of this residue in regulating PER stability, since early PER degradation allows early dCLK activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bioluminescence data and its relationship to PER stability.

claim: The dCLK active phase is shortened only in the S589A mutant, suggesting that inhibition of phosphorylation at S589 specifically accelerates PER activity (dCLK inhibition).
source: These data further demonstrate that the dCLK active phase is shortened only in the S589A mutant, suggesting that inhibition of phosphorylation at S589 specifically accelerates PER activity (dCLK inhibition).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bioluminescence data showing differential effects on the active phase.

claim: While both S589A and S589D mutants exhibit shorter circadian periods because of their effects on PER stability, S589A mutants exhibit a much shorter circadian period than S589D partly because inhibition of phosphorylation at this residue increases or accelerates PER-mediated inhibition of dCLK transcription.
source: In other words, these data suggest that while both S589A and S589D mutants exhibit shorter circadian periods because of their effects on PER stability, S589A mutants exhibit a much shorter circadian period than S589D partly because inhibition of phosphorylation at this residue increases or accelerates PER-mediated inhibition of dCLK transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined analysis of period length and phase durations.

claim: PER protein containing the S589A phosphonull mutation exhibits a steeper negative slope than wt PER, suggesting that S589A mutant PER is a more effective inhibitor.
source: We found that PER protein containing the S589A phosphonull mutation exhibits a steeper negative slope than wt PER, suggesting that S589A mutant PER is a more effective inhibitor (Figure 5C, red circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: S589D PER exhibits a slope statistically indistinguishable from wild type.
source: Consistent with our in vivo data, S589D PER exhibits a slope statistically indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 5C, blue circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The destabilizing effect of mutating S589, and the relative stability of S589D over S589A is in agreement with the stability exhibited by these mutants in vivo.
source: The destabilizing effect of mutating S589, and the relative stability of S589D over S589A is in agreement with the stability exhibited by these mutants in vivo (Figure 2C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing in vitro and in vivo stability data.

claim: S589A and S589D mutants inhibit dCLK-mediated transcription, with stronger transcriptional inhibition demonstrated by S589A.
source: Our data also demonstrate that S589A and S589D mutants inhibit dCLK-mediated transcription, with stronger transcriptional inhibition demonstrated by S589A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcription assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both S589A and S589D mutants exhibit decreased stability relative to wt PER, while the S589A mutant exhibits increased PER activity relative to both wt PER and S589D.
source: Our data demonstrate that both S589A and S589D mutants exhibit decreased stability relative to wt PER, while the S589A mutant exhibits increased PER activity relative to both wt PER and S589D.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcription assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The phosphorylation state of S589 delays the circadian transcriptional feedback loop in two ways: by stabilizing PER and delaying its degradation and by regulating PER-mediated inhibition of dCLK transcriptional activity.
source: Thus, the phosphorylation state of S589 delays the circadian transcriptional feedback loop in two ways: by stabilizing PER and delaying its degradation and by regulating PER-mediated inhibition of dCLK transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data showing effects on both stability and activity.

claim: When PER-SD sites are substituted with alanines to block phosphorylation (PER 4A), transcription is weakly inhibited.
source: When these sites are substituted with alanines to block phosphorylation (PER 4A), transcription is weakly inhibited (Figure 6B), consistent with the long-period behavioral phenotype seen in similarly mutated flies (Garbe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and confirmed by previous studies.

claim: PER 4A protein exhibits increased stability in comparison to wild type, producing relatively large amounts of PER.
source: This protein also exhibits increased stability in comparison to wild type, producing relatively large amounts of PER (Figure 6B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), again consistent with delayed PER degradation in the s-LNvs (master pacemaker neurons) of similarly mutated flies (Garbe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, and confirmed by previous studies.

claim: Phosphomimetic substitutions at the PER-SD sites (PER 4D) exhibit wild type-like inhibitory activity.
source: Phosphomimetic substitutions at the same sites (PER 4D) exhibit wild type-like inhibitory activity, consistent with wild type behavioral rhythmicity seen in similarly mutated flies (D. Garbe, personal communication, December 2013), but also exhibit decreased stability in our transcription assay (Figure 6B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, and personal communication.

claim: Blocking phosphorylation of the PER-SD delays PER degradation, while mimicking phosphorylation in this region reduces PER stability.
source: Thus in our assay, blocking phosphorylation of the PER-SD delays PER degradation, while mimicking phosphorylation in this region reduces PER stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcription assay data for PER 4A and 4D mutants.

claim: Mutations that block phosphorylation of the PER-SD exhibit lower transcriptional inhibitory activity, while phosphomimetic mutations are indistinguishable from wild type.
source: Functionally, mutations that block phosphorylation of the PER-SD exhibit lower transcriptional inhibitory activity, while phosphomimetic mutations are indistinguishable from wild type.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcription assay data for PER 4A and 4D mutants.

claim: The phosphorylation-blocked mutant form (S589A/4A) results in a stable protein that is a poor inhibitor of dCLK-mediated transcription.
source: The phosphorylation-blocked mutant form (S589A/4A) results in a stable protein that is a poor inhibitor of dCLK-mediated transcription, similar to what is observed when a small DBT binding site on PER is deleted (Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The increased inhibitory activity of S589A is muted when combined with PER 4A.
source: Thus the increased inhibitory activity of S589A is muted when combined with PER 4A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing S589A/4A with S589A alone.

claim: In S2 cells, the PER-SD region is phosphorylated without exogenous DBT or TIM expression.
source: In S2 cells, the PER-SD region is phosphorylated without exogenous DBT or TIM expression (Chiu et al., 2008), suggesting that PER-SD occurs before S589 phosphorylation, and is independent of TIM binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and inference about the order of phosphorylation.

claim: The first stage of phosphorylation represented by S589A/4D reveals a strong, unstable inhibitor that resembles S589A.
source: The first stage of phosphorylation represented by S589A/4D reveals a strong, unstable inhibitor that resembles S589A.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PER phosphorylation blocked at S589 is likely re-directed through Route I for degradation, while still maintaining its inhibitory activity established by a phosphorylated PER-SD.
source: Thus, PER phosphorylation blocked at S589 is likely re-directed through Route I for degradation (Figure 6A), while still maintaining its inhibitory activity established by a phosphorylated PER-SD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavior of S589A/4D mutant and the phosphorylation cascade model.

claim: S589D/4D reveals a PER variant that is a strong and stable inhibitor.
source: To determine the consequence of permitting S589 phosphorylation, we substituted both S589 and the PER-SD serines with aspartates (S589D/4D) to reveal a PER variant that is a strong and stable inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Analysis of purified PER fragments by SEC-MALS and SAXS revealed no change in the global structure of wild type versus S589D/4D protein, with overall shapes of the proteins approximately the same, and with little difference in their flexibility as determined by trypsin protection assay.
source: Analysis of purified PER fragments by size exclusion chromatography multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) revealed no change in the global structure of either protein, with overall shapes of the proteins approximately the same, and with little difference in their flexibility as determined by trypsin protection assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylation does not affect the global conformation of PER but may alter local structure in a manner that influences its function.
source: These data suggest that phosphorylation does not affect the global conformation of PER but may alter local structure in a manner that influences its function (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural analysis data.

claim: Phosphorylation of S589 commits PER to Route II, leading to a PER isoform that is stable and active through subtle changes to protein conformation.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of S589 commits PER to Route II, leading to a PER isoform that is stable and active through subtle changes to protein conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data on S589D/4D mutant.

claim: S589 phosphorylation is likely not blocked by PER-SD phosphorylation, but functions as a switch in delayed transcription in the circadian clock, committing PER to degradation or stable inhibition.
source: S589 phosphorylation is likely not blocked by PER-SD phosphorylation, but functions as a switch in delayed transcription in the circadian clock, committing PER to degradation or stable inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of various PER mutants.

claim: A PER variant S589D/4A is an unstable protein with indeterminate inhibitory activity that resembles S589D.
source: A PER variant not predicted by the phosphorylation model, S589D/4A, is an unstable protein with indeterminate inhibitory activity that resembles S589D (Figures 5C and 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 6C.

claim: DBT stabilizes and activates PER inhibition to delay transcription in the circadian clock.
source: In this study, we present a model in which DBT stabilizes and activates PER inhibition to delay transcription in the circadian clock (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: DBT begins phosphorylation of PER in the PER-SD, initiating inhibition of dCLK-mediated transcription by PER.
source: DBT begins phosphorylation of PER in the PER-SD (Garbe et al., 2013; Kivimäe et al., 2008) (Step 1), initiating inhibition of dCLK-mediated transcription by PER.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data and previous studies.

claim: S589 is subsequently phosphorylated to stabilize the PER/TIM inhibitory complex in its inhibition-active form.
source: S589 is subsequently phosphorylated to stabilize the PER/TIM inhibitory complex in its inhibition-active form (Step 2).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: S589 is phosphorylated at ~ZT20, after nuclear entry.
source: Although protein extracts from whole heads suggest that S589 is phosphorylated at ZT20, after nuclear entry (Chiu et al., 2011), the stabilization effect S589 phosphorylation has on PER is apparent in the s-LNvs after CT02 (Figure 2), and regulates the temporal delay of transcription reactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Upon TIM degradation, PER is released from TIM protection and is degraded after CT06.
source: Upon TIM degradation, PER is released from TIM protection and is degraded after CT06 (Step 3).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: The steps that delay dCLK-mediated transcription activity rely on the activation and stabilization of PER by DBT phosphorylation, before TIM degradation ensues.
source: Thus, the steps that delay dCLK-mediated transcription activity rely on the activation and stabilization of PER by DBT phosphorylation, before TIM degradation ensues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proposed model and experimental data.

claim: DBT is likely to regulate the stability and inhibitory activity of PER through separate mechanisms.
source: DBT is likely to regulate the stability and inhibitory activity of PER through separate mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing separable effects on stability and activity.

claim: Functional uncoupling of stability and activity regulation has been suggested for the Neurospora clock.
source: Such functional uncoupling has also been suggested for the Neurospora clock (Larrondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Regions near the N- and C-termini of PER regulate PER stability and inhibitory activity, respectively.
source: Regions near the N- and C-termini of PER regulate PER stability and inhibitory activity, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PER protein domains.

claim: Phosphorylation of S47 at the N-terminus of PER regulates PER-SLIMB binding that leads to the ubiquitination and degradation of PER.
source: Phosphorylation of S47 at the N-terminus of PER regulates PER-SLIMB binding that leads to the ubiquitination and degradation of PER (Chiu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The dCLK/CYC Inhibitory Domain (CCID) at the C-terminus of PER physically interacts with dCLK to block transcriptional activity.
source: The dCLK/CYC Inhibitory Domain (CCID) at the C-terminus of PER physically interacts with dCLK to block transcriptional activity (Chang and Reppert, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The two functional regions of PER correlate with the two predicted DBT binding sites that reside at the PER N-terminus (residues 1–365) and a third of the way from the C-terminus (residues 755–809).
source: These two functional regions of PER correlate with the two predicted DBT binding sites that reside at the PER N-terminus (residues 1–365) and a third of the way from the C-terminus (residues 755–809) (Kim et al., 2007; Kloss et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both long-period (dbtL) and short-period (dbtS) behavioral phenotypes carry mutations that reduce the kinase activity of DBT.
source: Both long-period (dbtL) and short-period (dbtS) behavioral phenotypes carry mutations that reduce the kinase activity of DBT (Kivimäe et al., 2008; Preuss et al., 2004; Price et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The S589 mutant flies resistant to the effects of a dbtS mutant background have periods that are lengthened in a dbtL mutant background.
source: Indeed, we show that the S589 mutant flies resistant to the effects of a dbtS mutant background have periods that are lengthened in a dbtL mutant background (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: dbtS genetically interacts with S589, while dbtL does not.
source: These data suggest that dbtS genetically interacts with S589, as inferred by others (Rothenfluh et al., 2000), while dbtL does not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction data and previous studies.

claim: dbtL and not dbtS delays PER degradation in cultured S2 cells.
source: Since dbtL and not dbtS delays PER degradation in cultured S2 cells (Syed et al., 2011), dbtS may affect PER inhibition function through its (in)activity in the S589/PER-SD region.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and inference about dbtS function.

claim: Distinct phospho-programs regulate human PER2 stability and inhibitor activity.
source: Distinct phospho-programs also regulate human PER2 stability and inhibitor activity (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The human study focuses on the hPER2 variants S662G and S662D, analogous to the PER S589A and S589D variants in flies, targeted by the mammalian orthologue of DBT, CKIδ.
source: The human study focuses on the hPER2 variants S662G and S662D, analogous to the PER S589A and S589D variants in flies, targeted by the mammalian orthologue of DBT, CKIδ.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on human PER2.

claim: Unlike S589D, S662D exhibits a long behavioral period.
source: Unlike S589D, S662D exhibits a long behavioral period.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on human PER2.

claim: The decreased levels of the hPER2 S662G mutant is primarily due to increased hPER2 inhibitory activity at the hper2 locus (decrease in transcription), rather than a change in protein stability.
source: Although both S589A and S662G lead to a reduction of PER or hPER2 respectively, the decreased levels of the hPER2 S662G mutant is primarily due to increased hPER2 inhibitory activity at the hper2 locus (decrease in transcription), rather than a change in protein stability.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on human PER2.

claim: S589 phosphorylation (S589D) stabilizes PER in complex with TIM and helps activate PER inhibitory activity.
source: On the other hand, S589 phosphorylation (S589D) stabilizes PER in complex with TIM and helps activate PER inhibitory activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Both S589A and S662G advance evening anticipation behavior.
source: Despite these differences, both S589A and S662G advance evening anticipation behavior, suggesting that phospho-regulation of these sites underlie this aspect of rhythmic behavior.
evidence: This is a comparison between fly and human data, with inference about the conserved function.

claim: A reduction of DBT activity in mutant flies (dbtL) or reduced CKIδ expression in mice (heterozygous expression) both lead to longer period behavioral rhythms that are independent of residue substitution in positions S589/S662.
source: Also, a reduction of DBT activity in mutant flies (dbtL) or reduced CKIδ expression in mice (heterozygous expression) both lead to longer period behavioral rhythms that are independent of residue substitution in positions S589/S662.
evidence: This is a comparison between fly and mouse data showing conserved function.

claim: Despite differences in the PER function that sites S662 and S589 regulate, both mammals and flies utilize distinct mechanisms that employ DBT/CKIδ to separately regulate the activity and stability of Period protein, delaying transcription reactivation in the circadian clock.
source: Thus, despite differences in the PER function that sites S662 and S589 regulate, both mammals and flies utilize distinct mechanisms that employ DBT/CKIδ to separately regulate the activity and stability of Period protein, delaying transcription reactivation in the circadian clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the conservation of mechanisms between flies and mammals.

claim: S589A/4D represents the initiation of the phosphorylation cascade that activates PER transcriptional inhibitory activity.
source: S589A/4D represents the initiation of the phosphorylation cascade that activates PER transcriptional inhibitory activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mutant data in the context of the phosphorylation cascade model.

claim: The previous model predicts that S589 cannot be phosphorylated when the PER-SD region is.
source: The previous model also predicts that S589 cannot be phosphorylated when the PER-SD region is (Chiu et al., 2011; Garbe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the previous model based on cited studies.

claim: If S589 cannot be phosphorylated when the PER-SD region is, S589A/4D and PER 4D would behave similarly.
source: If this were the case, S589A/4D and PER 4D would behave similarly.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the previous model.

claim: S589A/4D appears more like S589A and PER4D more like S589D/4D in the transcription assay, suggesting no antagonistic relationship between the two regions.
source: Instead, S589A/4D appears more like S589A and PER4D more like S589D/4D in our assay, again suggesting no antagonistic relationship between the two regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcription assay data.

claim: S589 is phosphorylated at ~ZT20, and appears to remain phosphorylated as PER is degraded.
source: In vivo, S589 is phosphorylated at ~ZT20, and appears to remain phosphorylated as PER is degraded (Chiu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The PER-SD region is phosphorylated before S589, based on mass spectrometry of PER isolated from cultured cells, or epigenetic data.
source: Other data suggest that the PER-SD region is phosphorylated before S589, based on mass spectrometry of PER isolated from cultured cells (Chiu et al., 2008), or epigenetic data (Garbe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PER-SD promotes S589 phosphorylation to stabilize and activate PER inhibition, and delay transcription by inhibiting dCLK, which peaks around CT02.
source: Therefore, we suggest that PER-SD promotes S589 phosphorylation to stabilize and activate PER inhibition, and delay transcription by inhibiting dCLK, which peaks around CT02.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and the proposed model.

claim: S589 phosphorylation is relevant after CT02 to stabilize the PER/TIM complex.
source: Indeed, S589 phosphorylation is relevant after CT02 to stabilize the PER/TIM complex (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Phosphatases play a role in maintaining 24 hr behavioral rhythms.
source: Phosphatases play a role in maintaining 24 hr behavioral rhythms (Chen et al., 2007; Fang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If phosphatases act on the stable inhibitor represented by S589D/4D, they can convert this PER variant to either an isoform represented by S589A/4D, or through multiple actions, to the S589D/4A isoform.
source: If phosphatases act on the stable inhibitor represented by S589D/4D, they can convert this PER variant to either an isoform represented by S589A/4D, or through multiple actions, to the S589D/4A isoform.
evidence: This is speculation about how phosphatases might act on PER.

claim: The re-formed S589A/4D representative isoform can be re-phosphorylated, pushing the clock forward.
source: In such a scenario, the re-formed S589A/4D representative isoform can be re-phosphorylated, pushing the clock forward.
evidence: This is speculation about the consequences of phosphatase action.

claim: The S589D/4A representative isoform would be rapidly degraded, disallowing the clock from shifting backward.
source: On the other hand, the S589D/4A representative isoform would be rapidly degraded, disallowing the clock from shifting backward.
evidence: This is speculation about the consequences of phosphatase action.

claim: The ordered phosphorylation of PER-SD and then S589 ensures that the circadian clock ticks forward.
source: Thus the ordered phosphorylation of PER-SD and then S589 ensures that the circadian clock ticks forward.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proposed model and speculation about phosphatase action.

claim: Mutations that block regulatory mechanisms of the circadian clock can cause significant health problems.
source: Mutations that block regulatory mechanisms of the circadian clock can cause significant health problems.
evidence: This is general knowledge about circadian clock disorders.

claim: DBT-mediated activation, stabilization and degradation of PER regulates delayed transcription during the day.
source: We have shown that DBT-mediated activation, stabilization and degradation of PER regulates delayed transcription during the day.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: Mutations that interfere with the delay mechanism shorten perceived day and hasten evening anticipation.
source: Mutations that interfere with this delay mechanism shorten perceived day and hasten evening anticipation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A single mutation that alters splicing of cryptochrome (transcriptional inhibitor in humans) alters its binding affinity to Clock, also changing the delay of transcription inhibition in humans to cause a familial form of delayed sleep phase disorder.
source: Similarly, a single mutation that alters splicing of cryptochrome (transcriptional inhibitor in humans) alters its binding affinity to Clock, also changing the delay of transcription inhibition in humans to cause a familial form of delayed sleep phase disorder (Patke et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.
